timelinePage.title: Where I've been
timelinePage.subhead: Roles, projects, and milestones — roughly in order. Click any card with more detail to see the full story.

contentLines: I grew up in a small village in northern Lithuania.

dialogData.text: I grew up in a small village in Lithuania called Moškėnai. There are only a few houses there, and a forest just nearby.
I spent a lot of time outside or curled up at home reading books.

contentLines: Even before finishing school, I knew what I wanted to do — so it was easy to pick my exams and decide on a university.
I took the required exams, finished high school, and got into the university I wanted.

dialogData.text: I went to school in the nearest city — Rokiškis.

My grades were never perfect, but I never had bad ones either. I liked the sciences — informatics, math, physics — and also English and history. A second foreign language (Russian) was harder for me, and I never became proficient at it.

For the last two years of high school we had to choose subjects to specialize in. Most people struggled with the choice, but I already knew I wanted to study information technologies, so picking was easy.
Before finishing high school we had to choose and pass exams. I took five:
dialogData.secondText: Informatics and Physics were my best results. After the exams I applied to university and got accepted by my first pick.

contentLines: I studied Informatics Engineering at Kaunas University of Technology.
Subjects included programming, databases, cyber security, mathematics, and statistics.

dialogData.text: I did my Bachelor's in Informatics Engineering at Kaunas University of Technology over four years.
The first two years cover more general subjects: math, physics, philosophy, statistics, data structures. After that the tracks split and the specialization subjects begin.
From the first semester we started learning C++. The course began with the basics, but the pace was fast, so you had to stay attentive to keep up.
The next year brought Java and PHP across several subjects. We also took a databases course, learning about different database types, normalization, and building one from scratch.
In the third year we had cyber security and embedded systems modules. We also got free elective credits — I picked API programming and game development.
My bachelor's project was a problem-tracking system for IT engineers. It was web-based, built with Angular and Material UI on the front end and .NET on the API side.

contentLines: After my first year of university I went looking for an internship.
I was still aspiring to be an IT engineer, so I joined "Baltnetos Komunikacijos".
By the end of it I understood the IT engineer path wasn't for me.

dialogData.text: I applied and got accepted to Baltnetos Komunikacijos — a company providing IT infrastructure and maintenance to other businesses. I assisted two engineers with their daily work.
I worked there for two months. I learned more about computers, picked up some maintenance tricks, and got a real feel for the day-to-day of an IT engineer.
But most of the tasks were dull and repetitive — usually ending in reinstalling an operating system. After thinking it over, I decided it wasn't something I wanted to pursue.

contentLines: The next summer I started another internship — this time as a Software Developer at Visma.
I worked on a team of four over three months, and stayed on at the company afterwards.

dialogData.text: After finishing my second year, I decided it was time for another internship — this time aimed at the Software Developer role.
I took the entrance test, passed, and got accepted for a Software Developer internship at Visma Lietuva.
I started alongside three other interns. The first two weeks were exercises focused on the fundamentals of programming.
When the internship ended, I stayed on and joined Visma Lietuva full-time.

contentLines: After the internship I joined Visma as a Junior Software Developer.
I worked at Visma for nearly two years, mostly on integrations.

dialogData.text: After the internship I joined Visma as a Junior Software Developer.
For most of those two years I worked on integrations between Visma's in-house systems.

I worked alone most of the time, which helped solidify my problem-solving skills. But it also got harder to improve without anyone pointing out what I was doing wrong, and there were stretches without enough work to pick up. The situation wasn't going to change soon, so I decided to move on.

contentLines: After leaving Visma I joined Devbridge.
I worked on a variety of projects there and grew into a Software Developer role.

dialogData.text: After leaving Visma and finishing my studies, I joined Devbridge.
I already had some Software Developer experience when I arrived, so I was assigned to a project right away. The stack was familiar: .NET on the back end and Angular on the front.
Devbridge is a services company, building products for other enterprises. During my time there I worked on four different projects.
My last project was a .NET microservices system built with Domain-Driven Design. The one before that was a Node.js project — plenty of variety and different challenges along the way.

contentLines: Since I'd been programming with .NET for a while, I wanted to formalize it with a C# certificate.
I finally took the exam in November 2019 and became a certified C# Developer.

dialogData.text: I studied for the exam using a Pluralsight course and a fairly thick book on programming in C#.
The certificate itself doesn't unlock much, but I enjoyed the challenge and learned some new things about .NET and the C# language along the way.

contentLines: At the start of 2022 I joined Railsr.

dialogData.text: After more than three years at Devbridge, it was time for a change. I joined the banking startup Railsr — a mostly back-end role focused on banking APIs.
I've been a Software Developer for a few years now, but the future still excites me — and I'm happy with where I am today.
